column2: Move the voltage selector jumper to the 3.3V–V position (number 2 in the photo).

Fit the DevKit onto the board: the DevKit's micro-USB port faces the DC jack side, the D23 label on the DevKit lines up with the board's D23 row, and all 30 pins go into the sockets. Press down evenly and slowly.
Never used the Arduino IDE with an ESP32? First do Stage 0 of the weather station guide: install Arduino IDE 2 and the esp32 by Espressif board, choose ESP32 Dev Module, upload the LED blink code.

Plug the USB into the DevKit. Multimeter V⎓ 20, black probe on a GND pin of the power block. Measure each pin in the right-hand column of the power block: note which reads about 4.6-5 V (the 5V pins) and which 3.3 V (the 3V pins). Mark them with a marker.
Also measure the V pin in any row: it must be 3.3 V. If it is 5 V, the jumper has not been moved.
Install the libraries in the Arduino IDE (Tools → Manage Libraries): Adafruit BME280 Library and DHT sensor library. Choose Install All when asked.
Peel off the protective paper on both acrylic plates (from a corner, using a fingernail).

Mount the four motors to the bottom plate with the T-shaped acrylic mounts and long M3 bolts. The motor shafts face outward, the motor can (the one with two metal legs) faces the center of the plate, as in the level-1 dry stack photo (Part 6). Tighten just enough; acrylic can crack if too tight.

Motor wire lengths (from the motor leg): the rear motor 19 cm (no. 25) (to the TB6612 at the front end of level 1), the front motor 6 cm (no. 26). Longer supplied wires are cut; shorter ones are extended with 26 AWG. Not soldered yet: solder one red and one black to the two metal legs of each motor. Heat only briefly, the motor's plastic melts easily.
If the 100 nF capacitors are ready, solder one between the two legs of each motor (ceramic capacitors have no polarity). This dampens the motor brush sparking that can reset the ESP32.
Twist each motor's red-black wires together so they are tidy and do not become a noise "antenna".

Join them per side: the front-left motor wires are soldered to the rear-left motor wires passing beside them, red to red, black to black, then heat shrink. Do the same on the right. Now each side has one pair of wires reaching the front.

Cut an F-F jumper wire into four 3 cm female-end pieces (two from each end; keep the rest). Solder them to the front ends of the four motor wires and heat-shrink, so they can plug into the TB6612 pins.
Fit the wheels onto the motor shafts: press straight on until snug. The top plate does not need fitting yet.

Your TB6612's pin headers are already attached, so no soldering is needed. Flip the board over: the pin names are printed underneath. On your module the order is, left side PWMA, AIN2, AIN1, STBY, BIN1, BIN2, PWMB, GND and right side VM, VCC, GND, AO1, AO2, BO2, BO1, GND. Note that AIN2 is above AIN1: match the names, do not guess from position.
F-F wires from the TB6612 to the S pins of the 30P board: PWMA→D25, AIN1→D26, AIN2→D27, PWMB→D13, BIN1→D32, BIN2→D33.
STBY and VCC to two 3V pins in the power block. GND (the one on the logic-pin side) to any G pin.
The 470 µF capacitor: long leg (+) to WAGO 6V, striped side (−) to WAGO −6, in the holes still empty. Reversed, it can burst.
The left motor wires (female jumper ends) to AO1 and AO2, the right motor to BO1 and BO2.
Lift the robot: put the chassis on top of a box or glasses so all four wheels hang free.
Plug the USB into the DevKit (table mode), then battery switch ON. Upload the test code, open the Serial Monitor at 115200.
Switch OFF. Servo wires: brown = GND, red = power, orange = signal.

Bottom servo (pan, looks left-right): orange to the S pin of row D23. Top servo (tilt, nods): orange to the S pin of row D4. Use M-F wires: the male end goes into the servo plug's orange hole (the outermost hole), the female end to the S pin.

Servo power from WAGO 6V/−6 to the head on level 3: cut green 22 AWG 26 cm (no. 19) and black 26 AWG (your UL1007 wire) 19 cm (no. 20). The two servos' current is at most about 1.5 A, so 26 AWG is enough for the GND, and black 22 AWG would not be any worse.

Cut the red and brown wires of each servo 10 cm from the servo body. Do not cut the orange wire and its plug. The servo plug stays a single 3-hole block: the leftover red-brown on the plug side stays attached to the plug, just insulate its end with tape. Only the orange hole is plugged in later; the red and brown holes are left empty.

Slide the heat shrink on first. Solder both servo reds to one end of the green wire, both browns to one end of the black wire. On the same joints, solder the second 470 µF capacitor: long leg to the red-green, striped side to the brown-black. Close the heat shrink.

The other end of the green wire → WAGO 6V, black → WAGO −6. 26 AWG wire is slightly smaller than the smallest size the WAGO grips firmly, so strip the black end 22 mm and fold it in two (11 mm doubled) before inserting. Tug gently: it must not come out.
Never power the servos from the expansion board's V or 5V pins. When moving, servos draw a large current and can make the DevKit restart.

Check the shared GND before switching on. Switch OFF and USB unplugged. Multimeter in beep mode (continuity): one probe on the G pin of the expansion board (DevKit GND), the other in a WAGO −6 hole. It must beep. If it does not beep, connect one wire from the expansion board's G pin to WAGO −6. Without a shared GND, the servo signal has no reference: servos move randomly or vibrate, the tilt may not move at all, and touching metal on the power line can make a servo move by itself.
Remove the servo arm screws first. Upload the test code. Once the servos are still at 90°, fit the arms so the head faces straight ahead and upright, then tighten the screws.

Switch OFF, USB unplugged. Set up the breadboard rails: the 3V pin of the power block → the top red line, the G pin → the top blue line. Two wires on the right side join the top rail to the bottom rail (blue to blue, red to red).
The 5V pin of the power block → hole a30 (column 30 becomes the 5 V point for both sensors).
Front divider: a 1 kΩ resistor (brown-black-black-brown-brown) at b3–b7. A 2 kΩ resistor (red-black-black-brown-brown) from c7 to the top blue line.
Wire a7 → the S pin of row D19.
Rear divider: 1 kΩ at b12–b16, 2 kΩ from c16 to the blue line. Wire a16 → the S pin of row D35.
Front sensor (F-F/F-M wires): VCC → b30, GND → any G pin, Trig → S of row D18, Echo → a3.
Rear sensor: VCC → c30, GND → G, Trig → S of row D14, Echo → a12.
Plug in the USB, upload the test code. Move your hand in front of each sensor.
This is the table setup. On the robot, the rear sensor is on level 1 at the rear end and its wiring is rearranged in Part 6 (TRIG through the breadboard because it is far from the 30P board).
Switch OFF, USB unplugged. Solder the pin header to the MPU6050 if not done yet. The MPU6050 will be stuck flat on the chassis later (Part 6). For now put it flat on the table.
MPU6050 to the I2C header of the 30P board (number 5 in the Stage 1 photo) with 4 F-F wires: VCC→VCC, GND→GND, SCL→D22, SDA→D21. The other pins (XDA, XCL, AD0, INT) are left alone.
Plug in the USB, upload the test code below (no extra library needed), open the Serial Monitor at 115200.
Make sure the scan finds 0x68. With the MPU6050 flat, pitch and roll are near 0 and the z acceleration is about 1.00 g.
Tilt forward-back (pitch) and left-right (roll). Past 40° the text MIRING appears: in the body code, that is the limit at which the robot stops.

Switch OFF. The top breadboard rails from Stage 5 must still be in place: the 3V pin → the top red line, the G pin → the top blue line, and the top rail joined to the bottom rail. Measure top red to top blue with the USB plugged in: it must be about 3.3 V. A 20 kΩ resistor (red-black-black-red-brown) at b20–b24. A 10 kΩ resistor (brown-black-black-red-brown) from c24 to the top blue line.
Wire a24 → S of row D34.

Shared GND: this divider measures voltage relative to the DevKit GND, so the battery GND must be connected to the DevKit GND. Switch OFF, connect WAGO − to the G pin of the expansion board with one wire (strip the wire end 11 mm to go into the WAGO, not an ordinary jumper pin). Check in beep mode: WAGO − to the G pin must beep.
The 6 mm button straddles the center gap: legs at e27, e29, f27, f29. The two diagonal legs are the ones used: e27 and f29.
A 10 kΩ resistor from a27 to the top red line (3.3 V). Wire c27 → S of row D39 (labeled VN on the board). Wire j29 → the bottom blue line.
Plug in the USB, battery switch ON, upload the test code. Also measure the battery voltage with the multimeter.
Calibration: if the multimeter reads Vm and the Serial Monitor Vk, the new factor = 3.0 × Vm ÷ Vk. Example: 3.0 × 8.10 ÷ 7.95 = 3.06. Note this number for BATERAI_FAKTOR in the body code.
Open robot_badan.ino. Fill in BATERAI_FAKTOR from Stage 7. If one side was reversed in Stage 3 and you did not swap the wires, change MOTOR_KIRI_TERBALIK or MOTOR_KANAN_TERBALIK to true.
Upload to the DevKit (board ESP32 Dev Module). Open the Serial Monitor at 115200, choose the line ending Newline at the bottom right.
Make sure the robot is lifted and the battery switch is ON. Type M 150 150 1000 and press Enter: all wheels go forward for 1 second then stop by themselves.

May be postponed: uploading the code above is required before Part 3. The safety tests below (obstacle, STOP button, time limit) may be done later in Part 6 Stage 7 with the robot lifted, once the table setup has been taken apart. Do not run the robot on the floor until all three are proven to work.
Type M 150 -150 500: the robot (if on the floor) turns right. Type P 45 90: the head turns.
Obstacle test: put your hand 10 cm in front of the front sensor, type M 150 150 1000. E DITOLAK must appear and the wheels stay still. Reversing (M -150 -150 1000) is still allowed.
STOP button test: press once, E STOP_DIKUNCI appears and the DevKit's blue LED blinks fast. All movement commands are refused. Press again to release.

Time limit test: type M 150 150 3000 and then type nothing. The wheels stop by themselves after 3 seconds. That is what happens if the brain hangs or the UART wire comes loose: the last command runs out and the robot stays still.
